claims.text: Machine-learning potentials trained on DFT data can accurately distinguish lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed approach will outperform earlier methods by capturing atomic-scale complexity and defect or impurity effects.
The relevant HfNbTaTiZr samples may contain defects or impurities, including approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Machine-learning potentials trained on DFT data constitute the proposed intervention.
The proposed approach is applicable below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K.
The proposed approach is applicable to defective or impurity-containing samples.
Atomic-scale complexity and defect or impurity effects mediate the expected improvement in heat-transport prediction.
Ab initio molecular dynamics is the mechanism underlying the proposed prediction.
The proposed method could reduce prediction error by 10–20% relative to earlier approaches.
The total thermal conductivity of an oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr specimen is 10–17 W/(K m) from 300 to 1200 K.
Deviation from experimental conductivity by more than 20% would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to reproduce the effects of defects or impurities on heat transport would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as machine-learning potentials trained on DFT data, whereas the mechanism is labeled ab initio molecular dynamics. These are distinct computational approaches, and the hypothesis does not explain whether the potentials accelerate molecular dynamics, supplement ab initio calculations, or are themselves being treated as ab initio dynamics.

The hypothesis claims separation of lattice and electronic heat transport, but the stated ab initio molecular-dynamics mechanism addresses atomic motion and does not specify an electronic-transport calculation capable of producing a separate electronic contribution.
